source.title: Revisiting LARS for Large Batch Training Generalization of Neural Networks
source.authors: K. Do; Minh-Duong Nguyen; Ho-Lam Nguyen; Long Tran-Thanh; Nguyen H. Tran; Quoc-Viet Pham

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, though some table headings and layout are garbled.
record.tranche_reason: It compares large-batch training methods and reports classification accuracy and test-loss outcomes, using a new optimizer and measurements rather than directly reproducing the original large-batch studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for LARS, LAMB, and TVLARS across batch sizes, but the flattened Table I makes dataset/task column assignments uncertain. It also discusses cited results from prior work; those are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own held-out accuracy across batch sizes 512–16384 on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, including classification and self-supervised training. These results bear on V5, although they do not establish recovery to a conventional small-batch baseline. Optimizer superiority alone does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that TVLARS improves convergence and often accuracy over LARS and LAMB on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet classification and Barlow Twins experiments, particularly at very large batches. They attribute this to early exploration and configurable decay; the experiments do not establish universal superiority or recovery to a conventional small-batch baseline.
record.recipe_differences: Proposes TVLARS, a time-varying layer-wise adaptive learning-rate method; compares it with LARS and LAMB. It does not reproduce the original large-batch generalization-gap method directly.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, decay coefficient λ, target learning rate, and weight initialization affect reported training outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: TVLARS often improves accuracy and convergence relative to LARS and LAMB at the same batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A configurable time-varying layer-wise learning-rate schedule can improve large-batch optimization; optimizer superiority does not by itself establish removal of a batch-size generalization penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: The preferred decay coefficient differs between 1K and 16K batches, and target learning rate affects accuracy and stability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: TVLARS hyperparameter sensitivity depends on batch size.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence (venue stated; paper text also says submitted for possible publication)
record.problems: The study does not report a direct small-batch control for its large-batch comparisons. Table I is flattened and task headings are not reliably assignable from the supplied text. Several plotted comparisons have no numerical values in the text. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Table I contains many batch-size, learning-rate, task, and optimizer entries, but the flattened layout does not permit reliable assignment of all values to task columns; the selected entries preserve one legible comparison without reconstructing uncertain mappings.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive methods versus SGD or momentum SGD under the specified tuning regimes. SGD is used in downstream evaluation, not as a matched optimizer comparator.

Language models, longer-training remedies, and recovery to a conventional small-batch baseline. Classification results cover batches 512–16384; SSL uses a separate 1000-epoch representation stage and 100-epoch classification stage.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, correlations with training–test gaps, and rankings against norm or margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Record the study's explicit finding that warm-up LARS deteriorates at exceedingly large batch sizes, distinguishing it from the separate warm-up versus no-warm-up comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Table I's four groups can be identified from its headings and VI-B as classification CIFAR-10, classification Tiny ImageNet, SSL CIFAR-10, and SSL Tiny ImageNet. Its 'ImageNet' headings refer to Tiny ImageNet. Additional table rows were explicitly declared omitted, so they are not duplicated in missing. The paper inconsistently describes initialization: Table I specifies Xavier Uniform, while VI-A specifies Kaiming Uniform. No uncertainty estimates support equivalence claims.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.

The study varies batch size and optimizer/learning-rate settings, but does not report a direct same-epoch comparison against small-batch training. Its results concern LARS-family methods, not language models.
No magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measurement or comparison with norm/margin measures.

rows.subject: LARS
rows.operation_detail: Large-batch classification training with LARS; reported accuracy comparison in Table I.
rows.note: Table I's flattened headings do not securely identify the task column; accuracy is recorded as printed without inferring the column mapping.
rows.check: 74.64 is the CIFAR-10 classification result at batch 512 and learning rate 1. This single endpoint needs a larger-batch comparator to establish a batch penalty. LARS is an optimizer, not a model. Weight decay is stated as 5×10−4 in VI-A; the table's λ=10−4 is not identified as weight decay.

rows.subject: LAMB
rows.operation_detail: Large-batch classification training with LAMB; reported accuracy comparison in Table I.
rows.note: The table placement supports the printed value but its flattened headings leave the task column uncertain.
rows.check: 57.88 is the CIFAR-10 classification result at batch 512 and learning rate 1. The LARS baseline compares optimizers, whereas V5 requires a batch-size comparison within a training recipe. LAMB is an optimizer. Correct weight decay to the stated 5×10−4.

rows.subject: TVLARS
rows.operation_detail: Large-batch classification training with TVLARS; reported accuracy comparison in Table I.
rows.note: The table placement supports the printed value but its flattened headings leave the task column uncertain.
rows.check: 78.92 is the CIFAR-10 classification result at batch 512 and learning rate 1. Its improvement over LARS does not establish removal of a batch-size penalty. TVLARS is an optimizer. Correct weight decay to the stated 5×10−4; the classification table specifies decay coefficient λ=10−4.

rows.subject: TVLARS
rows.operation_detail: Ablation varying the decay coefficient λ; the paper reports a generalization gap across target learning rates in the 1K batch experiments.
rows.value: generalization gap reported; exact values not stated
rows.note: This reports sensitivity to decay settings, but gives no exact accuracy values for λ = 0.01 or 0.005.
rows.check: This compares decay settings at one batch size, not held-out performance across batch sizes. The reported gap is variation among target learning rates, not a measured training–test gap or large–small batch penalty. The approximately 84% result is an accuracy under λ=10−5.

rows.subject: TVLARS
rows.operation_detail: Ablation varying the decay coefficient λ for large-batch training.
rows.value: models perform better with larger λ values; exact values not stated
rows.note: The paper states the direction of the result but does not give exact accuracy figures in the text.
rows.check: This compares decay settings at batch 16K. It measures recipe sensitivity without a smaller-batch comparator, so 'partial' is not justified for V5. The associated low-loss comparison concerns convergence and does not itself establish generalization.

rows.subject: TVLARS

conditions.value: Multiple target learning rates; exact accuracy assignments not reconstructed from figures

rows.note: The text says higher learning rates generally yield lower loss and higher accuracy, while noting that an elevated target learning rate can make the learning direction fluctuate in later training.
rows.check: Figure 7 spans batch sizes and approximately 100 epochs, so it is relevant to V5, but the supplied text does not preserve readable accuracy curves or numerical endpoints. Split this aggregate row into batch-size and learning-rate conditions before assigning an effect state.

relationships.condition: LARS with warm-up at increasingly large batch sizes in the CIFAR-10 experimental study
relationships.reason: Sections IV-B–IV-C explicitly report deterioration of warm-up LARS at exceedingly large batches. This verdict rests on the text; R1–R3 contain only batch-512 endpoints and R6 concerns TVLARS.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports deterioration of warmup LARS at exceedingly large batches, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet classification with batch-dependent learning-rate choices
relationships.reason: The declared omitted Table I results show no universal accuracy penalty: best reported TVLARS CIFAR-10 accuracy is 81.56% at batch 512 and 82.74% at 8192, while Tiny ImageNet rises from 39.64% at 512 to 42.08% at 16384. These are table-based comparisons, not conclusions established by R1–R6 alone.
relationships.display_finding: Better best-reported accuracy with larger batches was reported on both datasets, but these comparisons remain unverified and used batch-dependent learning rates.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 Barlow Twins representation training with TVLARS
relationships.reason: The declared omitted Table I results show best reported downstream accuracy falling from 70.54% at batch 512 to 50.15% at 16384 despite batch-dependent learning-rate choices. This verdict rests on the table rather than R1–R6.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports lower downstream accuracy with larger TVLARS representation-training batches, but this comparison remains unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Large-batch CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet experiments with LARS-family methods
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that LARS and LAMB performance deteriorates at larger batches and that TVLARS improves accuracy, but it does not directly compare against small-batch performance under a fixed epoch budget (R1–R6).
